extracted.intended_audience: experimental physicists / mechanical engineers and researchers studying friction, abrasion, and tribology
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and interpreting laboratory experiments measuring friction and abrasion between material pairs (metals, leather, ice, stone, machine bearings), including effects of pressure, surface, time, velocity, and unguents. Emphasis on empirical coefficients and guidance for machine design and materials selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friction varies with hardness of metals
rubrics_metrics.description: From the preceding experiments it appears: — that the friction of metals varies with their hardness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard metals generally show less friction than soft metals; experimental comparisons (Cavendish and Hatchett) corroborate that friction and abrasion were less in the hard than soft metals. Use material hardness as a central predictor when comparing metal pairings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard metals have less friction than soft ones
rubrics_metrics.description: That the hard metals have less friction than the soft ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is observed across multiple experiments and supports selecting harder materials (e.g., hardened steel) to reduce friction in delicate instruments such as pendulums and balances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friction of hard-on-hard (within limits) ~ one-sixth of pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: That without unguents and within the limits of 32lbs 8oz. per square inch, the friction of hard metals against hard metals may very generally be estimated at about one-sixth of the pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For design or estimation, when operating within those pressure limits and without lubricants, use ≈1/6 of the normal pressure as a working estimate of friction for hard metal pairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within limits of abrasion friction of metals nearly alike
rubrics_metrics.description: That within the limits of their abrasion the friction of metals is nearly alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When both contacting materials are operating within their abrasion limits (i.e., not being significantly worn away), differences between metal types in friction diminish; thus comparisons should consider whether abrasive wear is occurring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance increases markedly with higher insistent weights (specific range)
rubrics_metrics.description: That from 1.66cwt. per square inch to upwards of 6cwt. per square inch, the resistance increases in a very considerable ratio, being the greatest with steel on cast iron, and the least with brass on wrought iron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume linearity across wide pressure ranges; report the pressure per unit area and expect significant nonlinearity in resistance beyond low-pressure regimes. Include specific pairings (steel on cast iron shows very large increases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material pairing strongly affects friction
rubrics_metrics.description: Friction increased when yellow brass was tried. Friction decreased when cast iron was tried. The friction of cast iron on cast iron was still further diminished by hogslard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate friction as a property of the pair (A on B). Report and compare different pairings; consider testing candidate pairings under representative loads and with/without lubricants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of unguents (lubricants) varies with nature and load
rubrics_metrics.description: The diminution of friction by unguents varies as the insistent weights and natures of the unguents; the lighter the weight the finer and more fluid should be the unguents, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select lubricant viscosity/composition relative to contact pressure: tallow produced the least friction for yellow brass on cast iron in these experiments; soft-soap was second best and superior to oil; soft-soap combined with black-lead sometimes gave worse results. Report lubricant type and any pre-conditioning (fresh application, time at rest) because effects can be highly variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some lubricants produce irregular or load-dependent results
rubrics_metrics.description: Yellow brass on cast iron with anti-attrition composition of black-lead and hogslard, increased friction with light weights, and greatly diminished it with heavy weights, showing extremely irregular results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing composite or particulate lubricants (e.g., black-lead mixes), examine behavior across the expected load range; do not assume monotonic improvement. Record how lubricant performance changes with load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time effects differ by material class (metals vs fibrous)
rubrics_metrics.description: That length of time scarcely affects it (metals without unguents). Conversely, the friction of hide leather soaked in water appears to be greatly increased by time and weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish materials when assessing the role of time: for many metals (without lubricant) time has negligible effect after 'running in'; for fibrous/soaked materials (leather, cloth) friction can increase significantly with time and soaking. Include dwell/rest durations in experimental records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friction of fibrous substances increases with surface and time, decreases with pressure and velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: With fibrous substances, such as cloth, &c. friction is increased by surface and time, and diminished by pressure and velocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing fabrics/leathers, systematically vary contact area, applied pressure, duration, and sliding speed. Expect larger contact areas and longer contact times to raise friction; increasing pressure or velocity may reduce friction for fibrous materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: For harder substances friction ~ directly proportional to pressure (within abrasion limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: That with harder substances, such as woods, metals, and stones, and within the limits of abrasion, the amount of friction is as the pressure directly, without regard to surface, time, or velocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For hard materials operating within abrasion limits, model friction as proportional to normal pressure; area, time, and speed may be secondary. Validate proportionality over the pressure range of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: For dissimilar substances friction determined by softer material's abrasion limit
rubrics_metrics.description: That with dissimilar substances gliding against each other, the measure of friction will be determined by the limit of abrasion of the softer substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting contact pairs, assess the softer material's abrasion behavior; the softer material's wear limit will govern frictional behavior and should guide materials choice and lubrication strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friction generally greatest with soft materials and least with hard materials
rubrics_metrics.description: That friction is greatest with soft, and least with hard substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use material hardness ranking as a heuristic for expected friction levels; verify with experiments for each pairing and load condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity often does not increase friction (in these roller experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the result of these experiments it will be seen, that friction did not increase with an increase of velocity. The time in falling the whole height of twenty-one feet being double the time in falling half the height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In similar rolling/roller setups, sliding speed may not raise friction; report velocities and compare halves/whole distances to detect velocity dependence. Do not generalize—test for the specific geometry and lubrication state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial irregularity due to abrasion/run-in; conditioning reduces irregularity
rubrics_metrics.description: The irregularity of the resistances observed in the first seven experiments arose from the impartial contact and consequent grinding or abrading of the surfaces. The roller having attained its bearing, and the weight in the roller-scale being diminished, the irregularity ceased, especially when oil and tallow were used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a run-in period and report pre-conditioning (number of revolutions, loads) because initial abrasion/grinding can cause large irregularities. After run-in and with appropriate lubricant the motion becomes steadier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for apparatus friction and cord rigidity in deductions
rubrics_metrics.description: The deductions to be made for the rigidity of the cord used in the foregoing experiments under variable weights, as shown in the second and third columns, are nearly as the weights simply, and are applicable to most of the cases in Table IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and subtract apparatus-related resistances (cord, pulleys, bearings) from recorded forces. Provide a table of apparatus friction vs. load so others can apply the correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative friction coefficients for common material pairs (summary table)
rubrics_metrics.description: Table XV: Showing the amount of friction (without unguents) of different substances, the insistent weight being 36lbs. and within the limits of abrasion of the softest substance. Examples: Steel on ice = 5.87 parts of whole weight; Ice on ice = 5.70; Hard wood on hard wood = 7.73; Tin on tin = 6.85; Woollen cloth on woollen cloth = 2.30; Yellow deal on yellow deal = 2.88; Granite on granite = 3.30; etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide empirical friction-as-fraction-of-load values for representative material pairs under specified normal loads and abrasion-limited conditions. Use these tabulated values only within stated load/abrasion limits and experimental setup (36lbs insistent weight here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Friction of ice: weight dependence but irregular law
rubrics_metrics.description: From the foregoing experiments it appears, that with ice on ice, friction diminishes t increase of weight, but does not seem to observe any regular law with regard to that increase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test ice-on-ice across representative loads and temperatures; expect non-monotonic or irregular dependence and report temperature and surface preparation (air bubbles, smoothness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Friction of hide leather: soaked vs. dry behavior and surface area effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The friction of hide leather soaked in water appears to be greatly increased by time and weight. When the leather is not soaked, the resistance varies from one eighth to nearly one fifth of the pressure, and is diminished (ceteris paribus) by a diminution of surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For leather/piston-type contacts, report soaking state, dwell time, and contact area. Expect soaked leather to show very high initial friction (explaining large piston friction when first started); reducing contact area reduces resistance for dry leather.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stone sliding angles depend on dressing and mortar (relevant to arch equilibrium)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stones well dressed required angles of from 28° to 36° before they commenced gliding; with a bed of fresh and finely ground mortar interposed, the pressure on the centring commences at angles of from 25° to 26°. Other sandstones vary from 35° to 36°, and with mortar from 33° to 34°.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report stone type, surface dressing, and presence/quality of mortar when determining angle of sliding; include these data when using friction to assess arch equilibrium or masonry design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine design allowance for friction
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been customary to deduct one fourth of the power expended for friction. This allowance may maintain in machines newly set in motion. When the bearings have been equalized and the rubbing surfaces extended by the abrasion of the irregularities, the friction will be diminished ... But when the bearings are properly proportioned to the weight of the parts of a machine, and their surfaces kept from contact by unguents, a much less allowance may be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating required power for machines, provide an initial friction allowance (commonly 25%) for new/set-in motion machines; reduce allowance for fully broken-in, well-proportioned bearings and effective lubrication. Justify the final allowance with measurements or reference experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report measurement parameters and experimental conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables record: Weight on axle/surface (insistent weight), Weight required to move it (moving weight), Time, Proportion (parts of whole weight), Space passed over, Temperature (for ice experiments), surface area, and whether unguents were used (oil, tallow, black-lead etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing friction experiments, always report: material descriptions, contact area, insistent (normal) load, measured force to initiate and sustain motion, time/duration, sliding distance/space, temperature (for ice), and any lubricant type/condition (fresh, after resting). Include corrections/deductions for apparatus contributions (cord rigidity, pulley friction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer hardened steel where abrasion resistance is required
rubrics_metrics.description: The remarkable property of steel in hardening, and its power to resist abrasion, render it preferable to every other substance yet discovered in reducing the friction of delicate instruments, as is exemplified in the different experiments on the pendulum, and the assay and other balances recently introduced at His Majesty’s Mint and the Bank of England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For precision instruments and applications where low abrasion and stable low friction are critical, select hardened steel bearings/surfaces; document heat-treatment/hardening where relevant.
